Myths that sound scientific

Does crying always bring relief?

About half of people feel better after crying. The rest feel the same or worse. It depends mainly on who is around.

It is said that crying is good because it "lets out" emotions. Studies show something more nuanced.

What they found

In 2008, Lauren Bylsma, Ad Vingerhoets and Jonathan Rottenberg asked more than 3,000 people in 35 countries about their last cry. About half said they felt better afterwards; about 40% felt the same and around 10% worse. Those who felt better had usually been comforted by someone, and relief was more likely when the situation that caused the tears had been resolved.

Laboratory studies, in which people are made to cry with sad films, often find they feel worse right afterwards and somewhat better a while later. Crying has above all a social function: it signals to others that we need help. People with depression, on the other hand, often feel no relief from crying.

References

  1. Bylsma, L. M., Vingerhoets, A. J. J. M. y Rottenberg, J. (2008). When is crying cathartic? Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 27(10), 1165–1187.
  2. Gračanin, A. et al. (2015). Why only humans shed emotional tears. Human Nature, 29(2), 104–133.
